## Introduction

Words like "dimension" and "size" get used loosely when talking about arrays.
rray gives each of them one precise meaning, and uses that meaning everywhere, from function names to argument names to error messages.
This vignette defines each term.

We'll use this array for most examples:

```{r}
x <- array(1:12, dim = c(2, 3, 2))
x
```

## Axis

An *axis* is a single integer that picks a direction along the array.
Axis 1 runs down the rows, axis 2 runs across the columns, and axis 3 runs across the pages.

Many rray functions work "along an axis".
Summing along axis 1 adds up the rows, so only 1 row is left:

```{r}
rray_sum(x, axes = 1)
```

Summing along axis 3 adds the two pages together, so only 1 page is left:

```{r}
rray_sum(x, axes = 3)
```

Notice that only the axis you pick changes.
Every other axis keeps its original shape.

You can also give an axis by its [title](#titles) rather than its position.
See `?faq-axes` for more.

## Dimension

A *dimension* is the number of elements along one axis.
`x` has 2 rows, 3 columns, and 2 pages, so:

- Axis 1 has a dimension of 2.

- Axis 2 has a dimension of 3.

- Axis 3 has a dimension of 2.

To get the dimension of one axis, index into the [dimensions](#dimensions):

```{r}
axis <- 2
rray_dimensions(x)[[axis]]
```

## Dimensions

The *dimensions* are an integer vector holding the dimension of every axis.
They describe the shape of the array.

```{r}
rray_dimensions(x)
```

This is like `dim()`, except that it also works on plain vectors, which act like 1-D arrays:

```{r}
dim(1:5)

rray_dimensions(1:5)
```

In the other vignettes, dimensions are often written out in parentheses, like `(2, 3, 2)` for `x`.

You can change the dimensions of an array with `rray_set_dimensions()`, as long as the total number of elements stays the same:

```{r}
rray_set_dimensions(1:6, c(2, 3))
```

## Dimensionality

The *dimensionality* is the number of axes, which is the length of the [dimensions](#dimensions).

```{r}
rray_dimensions(x)

rray_dimensionality(x)
```

A vector has a dimensionality of 1, and a matrix has a dimensionality of 2:

```{r}
rray_dimensionality(1:5)

rray_dimensionality(matrix(1:6, nrow = 2))
```

The terms so far fit together like this:

```{r}
for (axis in seq_len(rray_dimensionality(x))) {
  dimension <- rray_dimensions(x)[[axis]]
  print(dimension)
}
```

## Size

The *size* is the total number of elements in the array.
It is the product of the [dimensions](#dimensions):

```{r}
rray_dimensions(x)

2 * 3 * 2

rray_size(x)
```

For an array, this is the same as `length(x)`:

```{r}
length(x)
```

Be careful not to mix up size and [dimension](#dimension).
Axis 2 of `x` has a dimension of 3, but `x` has a size of 12.

## Names

The *names* are a list with one element per axis.
Each element is either a character vector naming the elements along that axis, or `NULL`.
This is the same as `dimnames()`.

```{r}
y <- rray_set_names(
  x,
  list(
    c("a", "b"),
    c("c", "d", "e"),
    c("f", "g")
  )
)
y

rray_names(y)
```

To get the names along one axis, use `rray_axis_names()`:

```{r}
rray_axis_names(y, axis = 3)
```

The first two axes are common enough to get their own helpers:

```{r}
rray_row_names(y)

rray_column_names(y)
```

An array without any names has `NULL` names:

```{r}
rray_names(x)
```

## Titles

The *titles* are the names on the list of [names](#names).
There is one title per axis, and they show up when the array is printed.

```{r}
z <- rray_set_titles(y, c("row", "col", "page"))
z

rray_titles(z)
```

Titles are useful because you can refer to an [axis](#axis) by its title rather than its position:

```{r}
rray_sum(z, axes = "col")
```

## Broadcasting

*Broadcasting* is how rray works with inputs that have different [dimensions](#dimensions).
Axes with a dimension of 1 are repeated to match the other inputs.
Here, `b` has 1 column, so it is repeated across the 2 columns of `a`:

```{r}
a <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3)
a

b <- matrix(c(10L, 20L, 30L))
b

rray_add(a, b)
```

Broadcasting is important enough to get its own vignette.
See `vignette("broadcasting")` to learn more.
